question: How common are teenage births today?
why: Girls staying in school longer, wider access to contraception, and later marriage cut the global teen birth rate from 92 to 38 per 1,000. Still, about 12 million girls aged 15-19 give birth every year, mostly in lower-income countries, and in Sub-Saharan Africa the rate remains roughly 2.5 times the world average.

source.name: World Bank (UN Population Division estimates)
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (World Bank Open Data; UN Population Division estimates)

question: Is global literacy rising?
why: Reading is the precondition for learning, work, and using public services. The global aggregate partly relies on modeled or carried-forward country estimates where annual surveys don't exist, so progress is real but not annually measured everywhere.

source.name: World Bank (World Development Indicators, UNESCO Institute for Statistics data)

question: Is adult obesity rising?
why: Adult obesity has been climbing for over three decades with no sign of slowing: age-standardised prevalence among adults 18+ rose from 6.7% in 1990 to 15.4% in 2022 — nearly 880 million people. But for the first time, this is tracked through consistent global monitoring (222 million children, adolescents, and adults measured across 200 countries) and matched by genuinely effective medical treatments that didn’t exist a decade ago.

source.name: NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) / WHO Global Health Observatory

question: How many people have basic sanitation?
why: Sustained WASH programs and SDG monitoring expanded household toilets and sewerage, lifting coverage from 54.8% in 2000 to about four in five people. Yet roughly 1.5 billion still lack even a basic toilet, and much of what counts as «basic» is still not safely managed.

question: Is child labour falling?
why: Free compulsory schooling, social-protection and cash-transfer schemes, and ratified ILO conventions backed by labour inspection cut the share of children in child labour from 16.0% in 2000 to 7.8%. Yet about 138 million children are still working, and progress slowed enough that the world missed its 2025 target to end it.

question: Is child mortality falling?
why: Most of these deaths came from infections and birth complications now prevented by vaccines, antibiotics, and clean water — though the pace of reduction has slowed since 2015, from 3.9% to 1.5% a year.

source.name: UN IGME (UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group/UN DESA)
source.license: UN IGME/UNICEF data: free to use with attribution (UNICEF, WHO, World Bank Group, UN DESA Population Division)

question: Is child stunting falling?
why: Better access to food, healthcare, and clean water cut the share of children under 5 with stunting — chronic malnutrition reflected in low height-for-age — from about 33% in 2000 to 23.2% in 2024. But that’s the highest reading in four years: after bottoming out at 22.4% in 2020-2021, the rate has crept back up, and roughly 150 million children worldwide are still affected by it.

source.name: UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group (Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates)
source.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates, via WHO Global Health Observatory)

question: How many people have clean cooking?
why: Urbanization, expanding LPG and electricity networks, and SDG7 access and fuel-subsidy programs raised the share with clean cooking fuels from 48.9% in 2000 to 74.4%. Yet about 2.1 billion people still cook over wood, charcoal, dung, or kerosene, and the resulting indoor air pollution remains a leading environmental health risk.

question: Is global vaccine coverage rising?
why: Three doses against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis show whether the health system reaches infants.

question: How many people have electricity?
why: Electricity at home brings light to study by, cooling for medicine, and a connection to the world — yet as of 2023, 666 million people still lack electricity, concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.

source.name: Our World in Data (World Bank SDG7.1.1 Electrification Dataset)

question: What share of new cars sold worldwide are electric?
indicator: Share of new car sales that are electric
why: One in four new cars sold worldwide in 2025 was electric — a rapid shift away from oil-powered transport. But the progress is uneven: China is near 55%, Europe 28%, while the US sits at only around 10% — and even that slipped, with US EV sales down 45% year-on-year in Q4 2025 after federal tax credits ended in September.

source.name: IEA, Global EV Outlook 2026
source.license: IEA Terms of Use for Non-CC Material (attribution required)

question: Is extreme poverty falling?
why: Growing economies and wider access to work and social support lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Yet about 847 million people still live on less than $3.00 a day (the World Bank's new poverty line as of 2025, replacing $2.15), and since 2019-2020 the pace of decline has clearly slowed, hit by COVID and a worsening trend in Sub-Saharan Africa.

source.name: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, via Our World in Data
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (Our World in Data); underlying data: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform

question: What share of the world’s women are in the labor force?
why: The rate has recovered from its pandemic-era low (52% in 2020) — but over 34 years, women’s labor force participation has barely moved: 55% today versus 56% in 1990, even as education and economies changed dramatically over the same span.

source.name: World Bank Gender Data Portal (ILO modelled estimates)

question: Is Guinea worm disease almost gone?
why: The disease is stopped not by drugs but by filtering drinking water and controlling sources of infection — 2024 saw a small uptick to 15 cases before falling to 10 in 2025: the trend continues downward, but not in a straight line.

source.name: The Carter Center
source.license: The Carter Center, see source for terms

question: Are HIV/AIDS deaths falling?
why: Antiretroviral therapy scaled across low- and middle-income countries, generic competition that cut treatment costs, and wider testing reduced the age-standardized death rate by about two-thirds from its early-2000s peak near 27 per 100,000 to about 10. Yet HIV/AIDS still kills around 600,000 people a year, most in sub-Saharan Africa, and millions living with HIV are still not on treatment.

question: How many people have internet access?
why: Getting online opens education, banking, and the job market to people far from big cities — yet roughly 2.2 billion people (26%) are still offline, concentrated in Africa (~38% on average).

source.name: ITU, Facts and Figures 2025 (via Our World in Data / World Bank)
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (Our World in Data) / ITU data openly available for non-commercial use with attribution

question: Is global life expectancy rising?
why: The gain came not from one breakthrough but from sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics, and better nutrition together.

question: Are malaria deaths falling?
why: Mass rollout of insecticide-treated bed nets, rapid tests, and artemisinin treatment funded through the Global Fund cut the age-standardized death rate by about a third since its early-2000s peak. Yet malaria still kills roughly 600,000 people a year, most of them children under 5, and progress has stalled near 10 per 100,000 as drug resistance spreads.

question: Is maternal mortality falling?
why: Skilled care during birth and access to emergency help make the most dangerous complications manageable. The global rate for 2023 is 197 per 100,000 live births, but progress has slowed to roughly 0.5% a year since 2015.

source.name: WHO Global Health Observatory / UN MMEIG
source.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (WHO/UN MMEIG, via WHO Global Health Observatory)

question: Are people getting more schooling?
why: The spread of compulsory public schooling and better-educated younger cohorts replacing older ones lifted the world average from 5.9 years in 1990 to 8.8. Yet that is still short of a completed secondary education, and in the poorest regions adults average only about 6 years.

question: How many children get the measles vaccine?
why: Routine immunization programs raised first-dose measles coverage from 13% of the world's one-year-olds to 84%. But measles is contagious enough to need about 95%: coverage dipped during COVID and has not fully recovered, and outbreaks have returned where it slipped.

source.name: World Bank (WHO/UNICEF WUENIC estimates)
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (World Bank Open Data; WHO/UNICEF WUENIC estimates)

question: How much of people’s income does mobile broadband cost worldwide?
change: from 1.9% of income in 2021 to 1.1% in 2024
why: Competition among carriers, cheaper smartphones, and affordability policy pushed the global median price of mobile broadband down from 1.9% of income per person in 2021 to 1.1% in 2024 — yet people in low-income countries still pay roughly 19 times that income share compared with high-income countries, and 68 of 208 countries still haven’t crossed the UN’s 2%-of-income affordability line.

source.name: ITU, Measuring Digital Development: Affordability of ICT Services 2024
source.license: ITU data openly available for non-commercial use with attribution

question: Are deaths from natural disasters falling?
value: around 10× lower than a century ago
why: Early-warning systems, sturdier housing, and organized evacuation save most of those who once would have died.

question: Is neonatal mortality falling?
why: Skilled birth attendance, basic antiseptics, and newborn care made the first weeks of life far safer — the global rate fell from 37 to 17 per 1,000 live births between 1990 and 2024. But progress here trails older children: neonatal deaths now make up 47% of all under-5 deaths, meaning 2.3 million newborns still die in their first month every year.

source.name: UN IGME (UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group/UN DESA), via Our World in Data
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (Our World in Data); underlying data: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME)

question: Are fewer people getting HIV?
why: Condoms, antiretroviral treatment that makes the virus undetectable and non-transmissible, PrEP, and harm-reduction programs for people who inject drugs cut new HIV infections by 65% from the 1995 peak (3.5 million a year) — but progress has been uneven: the total barely moved from 2010 to 2015 (2.1 million both years), and the 1.2 million new infections in 2025 are still more than three times the UN’s 2025 target of under 370,000.

source.name: UNAIDS, Global AIDS Update / Fact Sheet
source.license: UNAIDS web content, © UNAIDS 2026 (no open/CC license stated on the fact-sheet page; see source for terms)

question: Is the ozone layer recovering?
why: Nearly all ozone-depleting substances were phased out under the Montreal Protocol, a rare case of countries jointly banning a harmful chemical; less ultraviolet means less skin cancer and less harm to crops.

question: Has polio been eradicated?
why: Vaccination narrowed endemic spread to two countries, but reaching zero means holding coverage — 2023 (12 cases) was a record low, then cases jumped to 99 in 2024 (Afghanistan and Pakistan) before easing back to 40 in 2025, still 3x above the 2023 low.

source.name: WHO Polio IHR Emergency Committee (GPEI surveillance)
source.license: WHO web content: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (until OWID republishes the series under CC-BY 4.0)

question: Is the global road death rate falling?
why: The global road death rate fell from about 18 to 15 per 100,000 people between 2010 and 2021, even as world population grew by nearly a billion and the vehicle fleet more than doubled — the result of safer vehicles, speed limits, and better-engineered roads working together, not one breakthrough. Still, about 1.19 million people die on the roads every year (92% of them in low- and middle-income countries), only six countries (2022) meet WHO best-practice legislation across all five key risk factors, and the rate even ticked back up from 14 to 15 in 2021 after the pandemic-era dip.

source.name: WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023
source.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023, via WHO Global Health Observatory)

question: How many people have safe drinking water?
why: Safe water at home cuts intestinal infections, one of the leading causes of child mortality.

question: Has smallpox been eradicated?
why: A disease that killed around 300 million people in the 20th century vanished completely through a global vaccination campaign.

question: Is solar power getting cheaper?
why: When solar power is cheaper than fossil fuels, leaving coal becomes an economic choice, not only an environmental one — though 2024 brought IRENA's first year-on-year uptick in LCOE in a decade, the long-run decline since 2010 (−90%) remains unprecedented.

source.name: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024

question: How much electricity comes from solar and wind?
indicator: Share of electricity from solar and wind
why: Solar and wind already supply about 13% of the world's electricity, up from 0.2% in 2000, but most of it still comes from fossil fuels, so clean energy is far from done.

question: Are fewer adults using tobacco worldwide?
why: Higher tobacco taxes, advertising bans, and pack warning labels under the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control cut the share of adults who use tobacco from 32.7% in 2000 to 20.9% in 2022. Yet roughly one in five adults, about 1.2 billion people (WHO, 2024), still use tobacco, and it kills more than 7 million of them every year.

source.name: Our World in Data (WHO/UN SDG Indicators Database)
source.license: CC-BY 4.0 (Our World in Data); underlying data: WHO/UN SDG Indicators Database

question: Are tuberculosis deaths falling?
why: Standardized diagnosis, free rifampicin-based treatment, and combined TB and HIV care scaled across low-income countries cut the death rate by roughly two-thirds since 2000. Yet tuberculosis still kills about 1.2 million people a year, and drug-resistant strains and millions of undiagnosed cases remain.

question: Is world hunger falling?
why: Rising farm productivity, incomes, and food-security and social-protection programs widened access to food, cutting the share from about 13% in 2000 to 8.2%. Yet roughly 1 in 12 people, about 673 million, still face chronic hunger, and the rate is still above its 7.5% pre-pandemic level.
